/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.headline: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.excerpt: The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document. A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”. Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success. Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027. Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.” The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels. It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.trail: Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda

/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.headline: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.excerpt: The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc. It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa. The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned. What is on the table? The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government. First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports. A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.trail: Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.headline: EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.excerpt: The EU executive has proposed a €45bn (£37.5bn) loan for Ukraine to help with a looming cash crisis and reinforce its defences, as Russia’s relentless bombardment continues. Announcing the plan to lend Kyiv the money in 2027, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table. And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.” She expressed confidence all 27 member states would stand behind the loan, despite four central and eastern European countries having already ruled themselves out. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he hoped for the swift adoption of the loan and was counting on the support of all EU member states: “Strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end,” he wrote on X. Zelenskyy convinced EU leaders last month that his country faced a €70bn funding gap in 2027. The EU pledged to cover €45bn and wants Ukraine’s other allies to cover the rest. Only 11 months ago, the EU agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, which was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s military and civilian needs in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia’s attacks have escalated, the cost of Ukraine’s defence and the toll of economic disruption continue to rise. Andrius Kubilius, the EU defence commissioner, said Ukraine’s military spending was increasingly dominated by drones.
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.trail: Von der Leyen says she wants to give Kyiv ‘strong hand’ in talks and is confident all 27 member states will back idea

/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.headline: EU ‘to close door’ to talks on long-term UK ties until Burnham has decided on Brexit
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.excerpt: The EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit, diplomats have said. European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal “reset” summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed. But they suggested a joint statement after a summit this Friday would signal that further discussions would follow on the UK’s entry to the EU’s energy single markets, irregular migration and a closer defence and security relationship. “Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK. Don’t come back until you know what you want. Work out what your options really are and then come to negotiate,” one EU diplomat said. “The prime minister needs to bring the public with him. We can’t have another negotiation based on just half the country. We’ll only put the effort in if we know it’s not going to change down the line.” Burnham is expected to set out his own next steps after the summit on Monday, including his hopes for a “national conversation” on what a closer relationship might look like. With less than 48 hours before the Brussels summit, negotiators were still racing to finalise Friday’s agreement.
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.trail: Diplomats say piecemeal approach of resets is reaching its limits and Europe wants clarity on whether Britain wants to reverse its exit

/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.headline: The leave campaign has been resurrected, so how should Burnham respond?
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.excerpt: The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even if the arguments were straight out of a familiar playbook. The video launched on X over the weekend, with scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians saying how desperate they were for Britain’s cash. Among Westminster’s anti-Brexit veterans, there was immediate chatter about whether a counteroffensive was needed. “I think the immediate reaction was – are they off to the races while we are still putting our pants on?” one said. For now, the rebuttal of Stay Out’s claims – including that returning to the EU would cost £750m a week – is mostly being done on social media by interested pro-rejoin freelancers, without any kind of central organisation. One MP said: “It is hard for us to begin any kind of new pro-rejoin campaign until we know exactly the direction the government is heading. “There are organisations that exist already, like Best for Britain, but I think making the case to the public would need a fresh movement. I think we want to stay away from the kind of marches that People’s Vote movement did with the blue berets if we can possibly avoid it.” Inside No 10, there is a confidence that Andy Burnham can make his own case for a closer relationship with Europe, without the need for any external pressure group.
/world/2026/nov/19/uk-eu-reset-talks-and.trail: No 10 is confident the PM can make the case for closer EU ties, while others worry about leaving the campaign solely in his hands

/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.headline: New law ‘may be needed’ after Google rejects call to remove Russell Brand’s YouTube prison message
/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.excerpt: A new online safety act is likely to be needed to tackle convicted criminals such as Russell Brand using social media platforms to broadcast messages from prison, Labour MP Jess Phillips has said. Just days after his conviction, Brand’s wife, Laura, broadcast a message from her husband to their 6.6 million YouTube subscribers, claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences for which he had been convicted by a jury. The video has had almost 850,000 views. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) launched an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules. Google, which owns YouTube, has rejected a UK government request, made via the Prison Service, for the video to be taken down amid warnings that it was causing distress to sexual abuse survivors. A Google spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.” Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, admitted the government did not have the power to compel platforms to remove distressing content of this kind. “Ofcom codes on women’s safety online are just voluntary and frankly voluntary codes to tech companies is the triumph of hope over experience,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.trail: Ex-minister Jess Phillips admits government does not have power to compel platforms to remove distressing content

/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.headline: UK ministers reportedly ask Google to block Russell Brand’s YouTube account
/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.excerpt: The British government has reportedly asked Google to deactivate Russell Brand’s YouTube account after he was able to publish a message claiming his innocence following his conviction for rape and sexual assault. A justice minister met representatives of the technology company to make the request after social media firm Meta disabled the former comedian’s profiles on Instagram and Facebook, according to Sky News. Earlier this week, the Ministry of Justice launched an investigation into whether Brand, 51, broke prison rules after he shared a message claiming he was not guilty days after his conviction at Southwark crown court. He was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. His wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her husband on Sunday in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel. Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, meaning that no criminal offence was committed in the release of the video. However, convicts are not permitted to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media. If he is found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a phone for a limited period. It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.
/news/2026/nov/19/prison-authorities-con.trail: Government makes request to tech firm in wake of 51-year-old’s prison message, according to Sky News

/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.headline: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.excerpt: In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading. With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months. Here’s a rundown of what we can gather after a big day for Anthropic and the AI industry Biggest IPO in history, but it’s not all good news Closing the day about 17% higher than its initial public offering price, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 when the market closed taking its valuation to roughly $1.7tn. The share price initially soared by 34% when trading got under way on Thursday, briefly taking the company’s valuation to more than $2tn. The blockbuster debut easily places the IPO as the biggest in history, with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s $75bn raised in June. Despite the excitement, major US stock indexes fells to seven-month lows on Thursday, dragged down by growing concerns about the longer-term outlook for the AI industry.
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.trail: A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges

/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.headline: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.excerpt: The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations. The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price. Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price. At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn. Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.trail: The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights

/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.headline: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.excerpt: Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX. Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each. When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn. Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.trail: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday

/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.headline: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.excerpt: The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed. How much are the shares? When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price. Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday. The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run. How do I buy shares? The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions. In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro.
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.trail: Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history

/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.headline: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.excerpt: Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom. The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to $78 a share. The California-based company will also raise a further $26bn via a separate private placement deal ⁠with cornerstone investors including the Google parent, Alphabet, and the chipmaker Nvidia. An extra $9.7bn could be raised from a so-called greenshoe offering, which kicks in if investor demand is high and would take the total amount raised by Anthropic to approximately $100bn if the shares sold at the top end of the price range. At the upper bracket of the $70-$78 per share price range, Anthropic would be worth $1.4tn on a fully diluted basis – which means taking into account all the common shares in the company in existence, including employee stock options. Trading in Anthropic shares is expected to begin next week. Investor jitters over the AI boom were crystallised last week when the US midterm elections produced victories for datacentre opponents.
/technology/2026/nov/19/anthropic-public.trail: Claude chatbot developer had been reported to be aiming for $2tn IPO on Wall Street before investors cooled on AI

/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.headline: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.excerpt: Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China. The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him. Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway. White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him. “Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article. “This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added. Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events. Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep.
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.trail: US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake

/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.headline: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.excerpt: Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac. But there was one exception: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi. The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official. The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment. Takaichi, on the other hand, was met off her plane by Zhang Qiyue, China’s former ambassador to Greece, a position below those who greeted other leaders. Zhang, though, does have a connection with Japan: her father, Zhang Shu, was once China’s ambassador in Tokyo.
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.trail: Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan

/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.headline: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.excerpt: In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow. On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage. The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US. All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy. A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”. “[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message.
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.trail: Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy

/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.headline: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.excerpt: Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency. The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence. He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025. White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained. The China leg of the trip will take place amid the continuing fallout from the Nvidia spying scandal, which prompted the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, to resign amid revelations he had had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.trail: Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.headline: Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.excerpt: Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine. The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion. Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end. Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead. “We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said. “It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.
/world/2026/nov/19/china-russia-us-agree.trail: ‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

/uk-news/2026/nov/19/lawyers-urgent-revi.headline: Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered
/uk-news/2026/nov/19/lawyers-urgent-revi.excerpt: Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape. Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”. He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”. The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”. Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person.
/uk-news/2026/nov/19/lawyers-urgent-revi.trail: Decision not to pause proceedings means £18m report does not engage with concerns over former nurse’s conviction

/uk-news/2026/nov/19/man-arrested-horrif.headline: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028
/uk-news/2026/nov/19/man-arrested-horrif.excerpt: Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties. Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases. He said one of the first elements of the bill to come into force would be the long-promised £250 cap on annual ground rent – though it will not be enacted as quickly as some MPs have pushed for. “The ground rent can be expected fairly early,” he said. “I think it will be a really historic moment … leasehold denies individuals control over the homes they live in and have paid for. “It then allows freeholders and managing agents acting on their behalf to extract excessive amounts of money from them, whether that’s unreasonable or extortionate charges, punitive and escalating ground rents, unjustified administration and permission fees – you name it. “Leasehold is an anachronism in the 21st century. I really do think that the bill that we’re introducing tomorrow [Thursday] marks the beginning of the end for the feudal leasehold system.” Pennycook and his Conservative predecessors promised to end the leasehold system, which exists in only a few countries worldwide and dates back to feudal property laws.

/uk-news/2026/nov/19/man-arrested-horrif.headline: Member of anti-migrant group found guilty of Staffordshire murder
/uk-news/2026/nov/19/man-arrested-horrif.excerpt: A member of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has been found guilty of murdering a man in a “completely unprovoked and unjustified” attack. Billy Allison, 36, delivered a “very, very hard” punch with the “stance and skill of an experienced fighter” which killed 44-year-old Matthew O’Gara while he was on a night out in Lichfield on 24 May. A jury of seven men and five women were not told of Allison’s link to Raise the Colours, which has been responsible for hanging hundreds of union jack flags on lamp-posts and roundabouts across the country, during the trial at Stafford crown court. Allison was also found guilty of grievous bodily harm with intent on Wednesday for twice punching O’Gara’s friend, 62-year-old Adam Cooper, on the same night as the murder, leaving him with a fractured eye socket and nose. O’Gara’s family thanked the emergency services who cared for him and said he remained “deeply loved” and “will always hold a special place in our hearts”. “While the conclusion of the court proceedings has brought a measure of justice, it can never replace the loss we have suffered or bring Matthew back,” they said in a statement. The trial heard how Allison had been drinking and had taken cocaine before he attacked the two men – neither of whom he knew. He had spent the day with his partner, Charlotte Dean, and fellow Raise the Colours members Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen and their partners.

/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.headline: Man arrested in Miami for three alleged rapes in New York’s Central Park
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.excerpt: Authorities have arrested a man in Miami who is wanted in connection with three alleged rapes in New York’s Central Park, including one reported last month. On Tuesday, authorities including the US Marshals took 30-year-old Dereck Rivera-Deleon into custody while he was working at a Burger King in Miami, New York City police said. Rivera-Deleon, originally from the Bronx, was arrested for “allegedly raping a woman in Central Park on October 24, 2026”, the New York City police department (NYPD) said, adding that he will also be charged with two rapes that occurred in the park in 2023 and 2021. Last month, police responded to a report from a 39-year-old woman who said a man threatened her with a knife before dragging her to a secluded area of Central Park and raping her. According to the NYPD, the incident happened at about 8.30pm near Fifth Avenue between 66th and 67th streets. The woman was taken to a hospital for treatment. The NYPD later released images of the suspect showing a man dressed in black, wearing a hoodie and carrying what appeared to be a backpack. Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, said in response to the incident: “What happened to this survivor is horrific. This is something that no one should have to endure.
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.trail: Man, 30, is in custody in Florida and awaiting extradition to New York for alleged rapes at park in 2021, 2023 and this year

/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.headline: Fifteen-year-old arrested in shooting near Florida university that injured 12
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.excerpt: A 15-year-old boy was remanded into secure detention in Florida on Monday charged with 11 counts of attempted murder following a mass shooting at a college homecoming party on Saturday. Six adults and six minors were injured, all but one with gunshot wounds, in the gunfire near the Florida Agricultural + Mechanical University campus in Tallahassee. It was among five mass shootings over the weekend – cases in which at least four victims were wounded or killed, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resource, has recorded 386 such cases in the US for the year so far. On Monday, the Tallahassee police department posted on Facebook that detectives had arrested a suspect in the shooting. The agency identified the suspect as Anthony Rivers III, 15. Police do not typically identify criminal suspects who are minors, though the severity of the charges facing Rivers made him an exception. He faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder and one of possession of a firearm by a delinquent after being arrested on Sunday, police said. Rivers appeared in juvenile court on Monday dressed in a white T-shirt and gray shorts. He was not handcuffed and did not speak during the brief hearing, during which Leon county circuit court judge Anthony Sheeran ordered him to remain in secure detention pending an arraignment.
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.trail: All but one of the victims sustained gunshot wounds as boy faces 11 charges of attempted second-degree murder

/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.headline: Florida police officer finds man dead and steals his house and identity, authorities allege
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.excerpt: A Florida police officer who discovered a man dead during a welfare check stole his house and identity and spent years renovating the property for himself, authorities said. Brian Louis Sguros, 35, an officer with the Lauderhill police department near Miami, appeared in court on Wednesday on charges including criminal use of a deceased person’s identification. Sguros was part of a team sent to check on a Lauderhill resident, Dennis West, in July 2022, after the department received a call from a worried neighbor, a press release from the Broward sheriff’s office (BSO) said. West was found deceased in the home of natural causes. Within weeks, the officer embarked on what BSO said was “a complex scheme to take control of the individual’s home” by involving himself in West’s post-death affairs. “Sguros represented himself to the Broward county medical examiner’s office as West’s friend, although there is no indication he knew West, and stated that West had no living family, which was untrue,” the press release said.
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.trail: Officer says he took possession of property and renovated it ‘to prevent criminal activity’ and ‘squatting’

/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.headline: Florida gambling helpline director sentenced to nearly 10 years over $1.4m theft to fund addiction
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.excerpt: A Florida man who stole more than $1m from his employer to bankroll a gambling problem – before becoming the director of his state’s gambling addiction helpline in trying to make amends – was recently sentenced to nearly a decade in prison. Bay county, Florida, authorities charged Philip Sullivan in March 2024 with stealing $1.4m from the Panama City Beach real-estate company for which he was the chief financial officer, Royal American, as local news outlets WMBB and WJHG had previously reported. An internal audit revealing numerous company credit card transactions that were unauthorized thrust Sullivan under scrutiny. He ultimately pleaded no contest to a half-dozen felony charges of grand theft on 16 October, when the Florida state judge Timothy Register adjudicated him guilty and sentenced him to nine years, eight and a half months in prison, court records show. Character witnesses on behalf of Sullivan asserted in court that he developed a gambling addiction after being prescribed the pharmaceutical stimulant Adderall around the time of the thefts. In March 2025, a year after his employment with Royal American ended, Sullivan became the director of 888-Admit-It, the Florida Council on Compulsive Gambling (FCCG)’s hotline, according to his page on the professional networking platform LinkedIn.
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.trail: Philip Sullivan, who sought to rebuild his life after gambling addiction, convicted of stealing from real-estate employer

/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.headline: Matt Gaetz accused in suit of sex trafficking two women in Florida
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.excerpt: The Republican former congressman Matt Gaetz has been accused of participating in the sex trafficking of two young women in a civil lawsuit filed on Thursday in district court in Florida. The allegations, which Gaetz denied in a statement to the Guardian, are the latest developments in a long-running sexual abuse scandal involving the politician who resigned from Congress in November 2024. In the 38-page lawsuit, filed in US district court for the middle district of Florida, the women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 claim Gaetz and two others “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts” from them “during 2017 through January 2019”. “The defendants collectively used their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of Plaintiffs to commit the acts,” according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit contends that the alleged victims “were recent high school graduates” at the time of the alleged misconduct. One of the defendants, Joel Micah Greenberg, a close associate of Gaetz, and the former tax collector of Seminole county, pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal offenses: sex trafficking of a child, illegally producing a false identification document, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud, stalking, and conspiracy. Greenberg was sentenced to 11 years in federal prison. Gaetz rejected the new lawsuit’s allegations in a statement to the Guardian.
/us-news/2026/nov/19/british-woman-flori.trail: Jane Does allege ex-congressman and two others coordinated ‘payments, drugs and travel’ for sexual acts
